decks.domain: Lane position, speed, curves, turning and following

cards.front: Why do drivers often misjudge how fast they are closing on farm equipment?
cards.back: Because farm equipment moves so slowly, the gap closes much faster than you expect as you come up behind it.

cards.front: On which North Carolina roads is farm equipment not allowed?
cards.back: Farm equipment is allowed by law on most North Carolina roads, but not on interstates.

cards.front: What lights must every vehicle in a funeral procession use?
cards.back: Every vehicle in a funeral procession must drive with headlights on, and with hazard flashers on as well if it has them.

cards.front: When may the rest of a funeral procession go through an intersection without stopping?
cards.back: The lead vehicle of a procession obeys all signals, but once it has crossed lawfully, or when an officer or funeral director directs it, or a police vehicle leads, the rest may go through the intersection without stopping, using extra care.

cards.front: Where do procession vehicles drive, and how closely do they follow?
cards.back: Procession vehicles keep to the right side of the road and follow the car ahead as closely as is reasonable and prudent.

cards.front: If an oncoming driver chooses to yield to a procession, what must that driver do?
cards.back: An oncoming driver may choose to yield to a procession, and if so must either slow down or stop fully off the roadway so other oncoming traffic can stay in its lane.
cards.memory_hook: yield means slow or pull off

cards.front: When may a driver going the same way pass a funeral procession?
cards.back: A driver going the same way as a procession must not pass it, unless the road is marked with two or more lanes moving in the procession's direction.
cards.memory_hook: only with two lanes its way

cards.front: How do the rules for oncoming drivers and same-direction drivers differ around a procession?
cards.back: Oncoming drivers may choose to yield to a funeral procession, while drivers going the same way are forbidden to pass it unless there are two or more lanes in its direction.
cards.memory_hook: oncoming may, same way must not

cards.front: What must an outside driver avoid when a procession goes through a red light?
cards.back: Never knowingly drive between vehicles in a procession, and when it goes through a red light, do not enter the intersection on your green unless you can do so safely without crossing its path.

cards.front: At an intersection, who may continue and who must wait when a procession passes?
cards.back: Procession cars may continue through an intersection behind a lead car that crossed lawfully, while an outside driver facing green must not cut across the procession's path.

decks.domain: Lane position, speed, curves, turning and following

cards.front: Which side of the road does the law require you to drive on, and when is the left side legal?
cards.back: The law requires driving on the right side of the road; the left side is legal only in cases such as one-way streets and passing.

cards.front: On a multi-lane highway, which lane should you use if you are going slower than the posted limit?
cards.back: On a multi-lane highway, if you are going slower than the posted limit, use the far right lane except when passing, turning left or avoiding an obstruction.

cards.front: When is driving on the left side of the road lawful?
cards.back: Driving on the left is lawful only in situations such as one-way streets and passing, while slower traffic on a multi-lane highway belongs in the far right lane.
cards.memory_hook: left only for passing or one-way

cards.front: What two things together set your stopping distance?
cards.back: Your speed and your reaction time together set your stopping distance, and higher speed lengthens both the distance covered while reacting and the braking distance.

cards.front: About how far does a vehicle going fifty-five miles per hour need to stop in ideal conditions?
cards.back: Even in ideal conditions a vehicle going fifty-five miles per hour needs about two hundred eleven feet to come to a complete stop.

cards.front: How does each extra mile per hour affect control and crash injuries?
cards.back: Every extra mile per hour reduces your control of the vehicle, and higher speed raises the chance that a crash will cause serious injury or death.

cards.front: How should your sight distance change as your speed rises?
cards.back: The faster you travel, the farther ahead you need to see so that you have room to stop.

decks.domain: Lane position, speed, curves, turning and following

cards.front: Why is driving well below the speed limit dangerous, and what must slow drivers still keep?
cards.back: Driving well below the limit is also dangerous; if you must go slowly, still keep to any posted minimum speed.

cards.front: Where is very slow driving especially risky?
cards.back: Very slow driving is especially risky just over the top of a hill or around a curve, where faster traffic may hit you before it can slow down.

cards.front: What should you do if a line of traffic builds up behind you?
cards.back: If a line of traffic builds behind you, it is wise to pull to the side, stop and let the vehicles go by.

cards.front: What do studies cited in the handbook find about vehicles going well under the limit?
cards.back: The handbook cites studies finding that a vehicle going well under the posted limit is far more likely to cause or be in a crash than one moving at normal speed.

cards.front: What speed should you aim for, given the risks of both speeding and crawling?
cards.back: Speeding reduces control and raises injury risk, yet driving well under the limit is also linked to more crashes, so the goal is a speed suited to conditions within the posted range.

cards.front: What two limits must your speed never exceed?
cards.back: Never go faster than the posted limit, or faster than is reasonable and wise for the conditions at the time.

cards.front: Can safe driving mean going slower than the posted limit?
cards.back: Safe driving often means going slower than the posted limit, but never faster.

decks.domain: Lane position, speed, curves, turning and following

cards.front: Unless a sign says otherwise, what is the speed limit in cities and towns?
cards.back: Unless a sign says otherwise, the speed limit in cities and towns is thirty-five miles per hour

cards.front: What are the maximum speeds for a school bus and a school activity bus?
cards.back: The maximum speed is forty-five miles per hour for school buses and fifty-five miles per hour for school activity buses.

cards.front: What are the maximum speeds outside cities and towns and on interstates?
cards.back: The maximum speed is fifty-five miles per hour outside cities and towns and seventy miles per hour on interstates.

cards.front: How does the default city limit compare with the interstate maximum?
cards.back: The default limit inside cities and towns is thirty-five miles per hour unless posted otherwise, while interstates allow up to seventy miles per hour

cards.front: Which two limits share the fifty-five miles per hour figure, and which bus is slower?
cards.back: The fifty-five miles per hour figure is both the maximum outside cities and towns and the maximum for school activity buses, while a regular school bus is held to forty-five miles per hour

decks.domain: Lane position, speed, curves, turning and following

cards.front: How should you handle your speed for a curve?
cards.back: For a curve, slow down before you enter so you need not brake in it, then gradually add speed through the curve to keep traction and control.

cards.front: If you must brake in a curve, how should you do it?
cards.back: If braking in a curve cannot be avoided, press the brakes gradually until you are sure steady pressure is safe.

cards.front: Should you do your slowing before a curve or inside it?
cards.back: On a curve, the speed reduction happens before the curve, and the speed is then gradually increased through it rather than reduced by braking inside it.

cards.front: When should you start steering into a curve, and where should you stay?
cards.back: Start steering just before the point where the road begins to bend, and stay on your own side as far right as you can.

cards.front: How should you prepare for a downhill curve?
cards.back: For a downhill curve, allow for gravity, shift to a lower gear before the descent, and brake earlier and slower than you would on level ground.

cards.front: On a downhill curve, when should you shift down and begin braking?
cards.back: On a downhill curve you shift to a lower gear before the descent and start braking earlier than on flat road, not once you are in the bend.

decks.domain: Lane position, speed, curves, turning and following

cards.front: How should you position and pace your car for a right turn?
cards.back: On a right turn, keep close to the right edge so no vehicle can squeeze in between you and the curb; slow before turning and then speed up slightly.

cards.front: Which road users are especially hard to see while you turn?
cards.back: Motorcycles and bicycles are particularly hard to see while you turn, so always signal and look before turning.

cards.front: How much space should you leave ahead on the open road?
cards.back: Following too closely is a leading cause of crashes; on the open road, leave enough space ahead that a passing vehicle could safely move into it.

cards.front: How does the two-second rule measure following distance?
cards.back: The two-second rule means leaving two seconds between the moment the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point and the moment you reach that point.

cards.front: How is the two-second following gap different from looking farther ahead at speed?
cards.back: The two-second rule governs the gap to the car ahead, while seeing farther ahead is what you need as speed rises, because stopping distance grows.

cards.front: On a multi-lane highway, which lanes should you check before changing lanes?
cards.back: On a highway with several lanes, check both the lane you are moving into and the lane beyond it, in case another driver is heading for the same space.

cards.front: What are the steps for a safe lane change?
cards.back: To change lanes, check the side and rear-view mirrors, look over your shoulder to clear the blind spot, signal ahead of time, and then move over.

cards.front: Why check the lane beyond your target lane on a multi-lane road?
cards.back: A lane change on a multi-lane road needs a check of the lane beyond your target lane too, because a driver there may be moving into the same space.

recap_hooks.text: Funeral processions drive with headlights on and follow the lead car through.
Oncoming drivers may yield, but same-direction drivers must not pass without two lanes.
Drive on the right, and slower traffic keeps to the far right lane.
Speed plus reaction time sets stopping distance, so look farther ahead as you go faster.
Too slow is dangerous too, especially over hills and around curves.
Go slower than the limit when needed, but never faster.
Towns default to thirty-five, rural roads fifty-five, interstates seventy.
School buses top out at forty-five; activity buses at fifty-five.
Slow before the curve, then ease the speed up through it.
On downhill curves, shift down before the descent and brake early.
Keep two seconds behind the vehicle ahead.
Mirrors, shoulder check, signal, and check the lane beyond before you move.
